outcomes.text: Pay attention to objectivity and to accuracy, precision, repeatability and reproducibility.
Understand that methods and theories change with new evidence, and why publishing and peer review matter.
Evaluate risks.
Ask questions and develop a line of enquiry from real-world observations plus prior knowledge.
Make predictions using scientific knowledge and understanding.
Select, plan and carry out suitable enquiries to test predictions, identifying independent, dependent and control variables.
Use suitable techniques, apparatus and materials in fieldwork and lab work, with attention to health and safety.
Make and record observations and measurements by various methods, evaluate method reliability and suggest improvements.
Apply sampling techniques.
Apply mathematical concepts and calculate results.
Present observations and data using suitable methods, including tables and graphs.
Interpret data, spot patterns and draw conclusions.
Give reasoned explanations, relating data to predictions and hypotheses.
Evaluate data, recognising possible random and systematic error.
Identify further questions arising from results.
Understand and use SI units and IUPAC chemical nomenclature.
Use and derive simple equations and carry out suitable calculations.
Do basic data analysis, including simple statistical techniques.

topics.title: Structure and function of living organisms

outcomes.text: Describe cells as the basic unit of living things and observe, interpret and record cell structure with a light microscope.
State the functions of the cell wall, membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, vacuole, mitochondria and chloroplasts.
Compare plant and animal cells.
Explain the role of diffusion in moving materials in and between cells.
Describe structural adaptations of some unicellular organisms.
Describe how multicellular organisms are organised from cells to tissues, organs, systems and organisms.
Describe the human skeleton's structure and functions: support, protection, movement and making blood cells.
Explain biomechanics: how skeleton and muscles interact, including measuring force from different muscles.
Describe muscle function and give examples of antagonistic muscles.
Describe a healthy diet's contents (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water) and why each is needed.
Calculate energy requirements in a healthy daily diet.
Describe consequences of dietary imbalance, including obesity, starvation and deficiency diseases.
Describe the tissues and organs of the human digestive system, their adaptations, and how food is digested, with enzymes as biological catalysts.
Explain the importance of bacteria in the human digestive system.
Describe how plants make carbohydrates by photosynthesis in leaves and take in minerals and water through roots.
Describe the structure and functions of the human gas exchange system, including adaptations.
Explain breathing with a pressure model, including simple lung volume measurements.
Describe the impact of exercise, asthma and smoking on gas exchange.
Describe the role of leaf stomata in gas exchange in plants.
Describe human reproduction: male and female reproductive systems, menstrual cycle (no hormone detail), gametes, fertilisation, gestation and birth.
Explain how maternal lifestyle affects the foetus through the placenta.
Describe plant reproduction: flower structure, wind and insect pollination, fertilisation, seed and fruit formation and dispersal.
Investigate some seed dispersal mechanisms quantitatively.
Describe the effects of recreational drugs, including substance misuse, on behaviour, health and life processes.
State the reactants and products of photosynthesis and give a word summary.
Explain how almost all life depends on photosynthetic organisms using sunlight to build energy-storing organic molecules and keep oxygen and carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere.
Describe adaptations of leaves for photosynthesis.
Describe aerobic and anaerobic respiration as breaking down organic molecules to power life's chemical processes.
Give the word summary for aerobic respiration.
Describe anaerobic respiration in humans and micro-organisms, including fermentation, with its word summary.
Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in reactants, products and implications for the organism.
Explain interdependence of organisms in an ecosystem, including food webs and insect-pollinated crops.
Explain why insect pollination matters for human food security.
Explain how organisms affect and are affected by their environment, including accumulation of toxic materials.
Describe heredity as the passing of genetic information between generations.
Use a simple model of chromosomes, genes and DNA, including the roles of Watson, Crick, Wilkins and Franklin.
Describe differences between species.
Describe continuous and discontinuous variation within a species, including measuring and graphing it.
Explain how variation lets some organisms compete better, which can drive natural selection.
Explain how environmental change can leave individuals or species less adapted and lead to extinction.
Explain the importance of biodiversity and of gene banks for preserving hereditary material.
Describe properties of solids, liquids and gases using the particle model, including gas pressure.
Explain changes of state using the particle model.
Describe a simple Dalton atomic model.
Tell atoms, elements and compounds apart.
Use chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds.
Explain conservation of mass in changes of state and chemical reactions.
Explain the idea of a pure substance and how pure substances are identified.
Describe mixtures, including dissolving.
Explain diffusion using the particle model.
Describe simple separation techniques: filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography.
Describe chemical reactions as rearrangement of atoms.
Represent reactions using formulae and equations.
Describe combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions.
Explain what catalysts do.
Define acids and alkalis in terms of neutralisation reactions.
Use the pH scale and indicators to measure acidity and alkalinity.
Describe acid reactions with metals making a salt plus hydrogen.
Describe acid reactions with alkalis making a salt plus water.
Describe energy changes on changes of state, qualitatively.
Describe exothermic and endothermic reactions, qualitatively.
Describe the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements.
Explain the principles behind Mendeleev's Periodic Table.
Describe periods, groups, metals and non-metals in the Periodic Table.
Predict patterns in reactions using the Periodic Table.
Describe the properties of metals and non-metals.
Describe the acidic or basic chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides.
Place metals and carbon in the reactivity series.
Explain how carbon is used to obtain metals from their oxides.
Describe the properties of ceramics, polymers and composites, qualitatively.
Describe the composition and structure of the Earth.
Explain the rock cycle and formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks.
Explain that Earth is a source of limited resources and how effective recycling is.
Describe the carbon cycle.
Describe the composition of the atmosphere.
Explain how human production of carbon dioxide affects climate.
Compare energy values of foods from labels in kJ.
Compare appliance power ratings in W and kW.
Compare amounts of energy transferred in J, kJ and kW hour.
Work with domestic fuel bills, fuel use and costs.
Describe fuels and energy resources.
Explain that simple machines give bigger force for smaller movement and vice versa, with force times displacement unchanged.
Explain heating and thermal equilibrium: energy passes from hotter to cooler by conduction or radiation, reducing the difference, and how insulators work.
Identify other energy-transfer processes: changing motion, dropping an object, completing a circuit, stretching a spring, metabolising food and burning fuels.
Treat energy as a quantity that can be calculated, with the same total before and after a change.
Compare start and end conditions of a system and describe energy changes in movement, temperature, position in a field, elastic distortion and chemical composition.
Use physical processes and mechanisms, not energy alone, to explain the steps bringing about changes.
Use average speed = distance / time.
Represent a journey on a distance-time graph.
Describe relative motion, such as trains and cars passing.
Describe forces as pushes or pulls from interaction between two objects.
Use force arrows, add forces in one dimension, and tell balanced from unbalanced forces.
Describe a moment as the turning effect of a force.
Describe forces that deform objects, friction, pushing aside, and air and water resistance.
Measure forces in newtons and measure stretch or compression as force changes.
Describe the linear force-extension relation and Hooke's Law as a special case.
Relate work done to energy changes on deformation.
Describe non-contact forces: gravity on Earth and in space, magnetic forces and static electric forces.
Explain that atmospheric pressure falls with height as the weight of air above decreases.
Explain that liquid pressure rises with depth, and describe upthrust, floating and sinking.
Define pressure as force over area acting normal to a surface.
Explain opposing forces and equilibrium, such as a weight held by a stretched spring or supported on a compressed surface.
Explain qualitatively that forces are needed to start, stop or change speed or direction, depending on force direction and size.
Describe water waves as transverse undulations that can reflect, add or cancel (superposition).
Describe sound frequency in hertz, echoes, reflection and absorption.
Explain that sound needs a medium, its speed in air, water and solids, and that sound waves are longitudinal.
Explain how vibrations produce sound, how microphones and the ear detect it, and the hearing range of humans and animals.
Explain pressure waves transferring energy, such as ultrasound for cleaning and physiotherapy.
Explain how waves carry information converted to electrical signals by a microphone.
Compare light waves with waves in matter.
Describe light travelling through a vacuum and the speed of light.
Describe transmission of light: absorption, diffuse scattering and specular reflection.
Use the ray model to explain mirror images, pinhole cameras, refraction, convex lenses (qualitative) and the human eye.
Explain light transferring energy from source to absorber, with chemical and electrical effects in the retina and cameras.
Explain colour through light frequencies, white light and prisms, and colour effects in absorption and diffuse reflection (qualitative).
Describe electric current in amperes, series and parallel circuits, currents adding at branches, and current as flow of charge.
Describe potential difference in volts and battery and bulb ratings, and resistance in ohms as p.d. over current.
Compare resistance of conducting and insulating components quantitatively.
Explain charge separation by rubbing as electron transfer, and forces between charged objects.
Describe the electric field as forces acting across space between objects not in contact.
Describe magnetic poles, attraction and repulsion.
Plot magnetic fields with a compass and show them with field lines.
Describe Earth's magnetism, the compass and navigation.
Describe the magnetic effect of a current, electromagnets and the principles of D.C. motors.
Explain conservation of material and mass, and reversibility, in melting, freezing, evaporation, sublimation, condensation and dissolving.
Compare solids, liquids and gases, including density differences.
Describe Brownian motion in gases and diffusion in liquids and gases driven by concentration differences.
Tell chemical changes from physical changes.
Explain changes of state, shape and density by particle arrangement, motion and closeness, including the ice-water anomaly.
Describe atoms and molecules as particles.
Describe how particle motion and spacing change with temperature.
Describe internal energy stored in materials.
Use weight = mass x gravitational field strength (g = 10 N/kg on Earth, different elsewhere).
Describe gravity between Earth and Moon and Earth and Sun, qualitatively.
Describe the Sun as a star, other stars in our galaxy and other galaxies.
Explain seasons and day length through Earth's tilt, in different hemispheres.
Use the light year as a unit of astronomical distance.
